name: Key Gompa Chham festival
when: June–July, dates set each year by the monastery on the Tibetan lunar calendar
summary: Once a year the monks of Key Gompa, Spiti's largest monastery, perform the chham masked dance in the courtyard below the prayer halls. Villagers from Kibber, Key and Kaza come in their best clothes, and the day ends with a ritual offering carried out and destroyed to drive away harm.
body: Chham, or cham, is the masked dance of Tibetan Buddhist monasteries: a ritual performed by monks in silk costumes and painted masks of protector deities, animals and skeleton figures, to music from long horns, cymbals and drums. Its purpose is religious. The dances show the victory of the teachings over obstacles and prepare the community for the year ahead.

Key Gompa belongs to the Gelug school and sits at about 4,166 m above the Spiti river, 12 km from Kaza. Its chham is usually held in June or July, on dates the monastery fixes from the lunar calendar. The courtyard and the roofs around it fill early. Families from Kibber and Kaza come dressed in traditional robes and jewellery, and stalls sell tea and snacks below the gompa.

The day is long, with slow, deliberate dances through the morning and afternoon. Towards the end, a torma, a ritual figure made of dough and butter, is carried out of the monastery and destroyed, a symbolic casting out of harm. Dates change every year and are announced only weeks ahead, so check current status before you travel and keep a flexible day in your plan.
tips: Come up from Kaza by 8 am to find a place to sit; take a taxi or the local bus towards Kibber.
Do not step into the dance area, and never use flash; follow any photography limits the monks announce.
Sleep in Kaza the night before, not Kibber, unless you have already spent two nights above 3,600 m.

faqs.q: When is the Key Gompa festival?
faqs.a: It is usually held in June or July, on dates set each year by the monastery from the Tibetan lunar calendar. Dates are often confirmed only a few weeks ahead, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can tourists watch the chham at Key?
faqs.a: Yes, visitors are welcome to watch quietly. Dress modestly, sit where locals indicate, keep off the dance ground and ask before photographing people.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for the Key festival?
faqs.a: There is no ticket. A donation to the monastery is welcome, and you will pay for tea and food at the stalls.

faqs.q: How do I reach Key Gompa on festival day?
faqs.a: Key is about 12 km from Kaza, around 30 minutes by taxi. Taxis are in demand on festival day, so book through the Kaza taxi union the evening before or share with others.

name: Ladarcha fair, Kaza
when: August, usually in the third week; announced by the district administration
summary: Ladarcha began as a summer trade fair where traders from Spiti, Ladakh, Kinnaur and Rampur exchanged wool, salt, horses and grain. Today it is Spiti's biggest public fair, held over a few days on the Kaza ground with folk dance, sport, stalls and visitors from every village.
body: For centuries Spiti sat on trade paths linking Ladakh and western Tibet with Kinnaur and the Sutlej valley. Ladarcha was where those paths met for a summer market. Traders brought wool, salt and animals from the north, and grain, cloth and metal goods from the south, and the fair was held for many years on a high meadow on the old route north of Kibber before it moved down to Kaza.

Today the Ladarcha fair is organised in Kaza, usually over three days in the third week of August. The ground below the town fills with stalls selling woollens, dried apricots, utensils and clothing, and the evenings bring cultural programmes with Spitian, Kinnauri and Lahauli folk dances in traditional dress. There are sports, government stalls and a steady crowd from Pin, Kibber, Tabo and the villages.

For travellers it is the easiest time to see Spiti's communities gathered in one place and to hear its songs. Kaza's rooms are full, and August is also the month of landslides on the approach roads, so book early and keep a spare day. Dates are announced each year by the district administration; check current status before you travel.
tips: Book Kaza rooms early or stay in Rangrik, Kibber or Langza if you are already acclimatised.
The evening cultural programmes are the highlight; carry a warm layer as temperatures drop fast after sunset.
Buy local woollens and dried fruit from village stalls rather than outside sellers.

faqs.q: When is the Ladarcha fair held?
faqs.a: Usually in the third week of August, over about three days in Kaza. The district administration announces dates each year, so check current status before you travel.
Ladarcha is the name of the old trade fair and its meeting ground on the route north of Kibber. Today the fair carries the name although it is held in Kaza.

faqs.q: Is the Ladarcha fair worth planning a trip around?
faqs.a: If you want folk dance, local dress and crowds of villagers, yes. If you prefer quiet, avoid those days, as Kaza's rooms and taxis are busy.

faqs.q: Is August a safe time to travel to Spiti for the fair?
faqs.a: Inside Spiti the weather is usually dry, but monsoon landslides can close the Kinnaur and Manali approach roads for hours or days. Keep a spare day and follow road news.

name: Halda, Lahaul
when: January, around the Lahauli new year; dates fixed by lamas each year (lunar)
summary: Halda is Lahaul's winter festival of light. In the coldest weeks of the year, families in the Keylong area carry bundles of burning cedar wood out of their homes to a chosen spot, and celebrate with food and visits. It is tied to the goddess of wealth, Shiskar Apa.
body: Halda is celebrated in Lahaul in January, in the middle of the long winter when snow covers the fields and families are at home. It is associated with the Lahauli new year and with Shiskar Apa, the goddess of wealth. The exact date is fixed each year by lamas from the lunar calendar, and it is celebrated in the Bhaga and Chandra valleys around Keylong.

On the night of Halda, people from each house carry flaming torches of cedar branches, the halda, to a spot chosen for the village, where they are thrown together into a fire. Prayers are said, and the following days are for family meals, special foods and visits between houses. Like many festivals across the Himalaya, it marks the turning of the year and asks for a good harvest ahead.

Halda is a community festival, not a show for visitors. Since the Atal Tunnel opened in 2020, Lahaul can be reached in winter when the tunnel is open, but Keylong is very cold and services are limited. Go only if you have a local contact, warm gear and a flexible return. Check current status before you travel.
tips: Go with a local family or operator who can tell you when and where the village fire will be lit.
Keep a respectful distance and ask before photographing anyone carrying the torches.
Check whether the Atal Tunnel is open to tourist vehicles on your travel day; snow can close the approach.

faqs.q: When is Halda celebrated in Lahaul?
faqs.a: In January, around the Lahauli new year. Lamas fix the exact date each year from the lunar calendar, so it moves. Check current status before you travel.
Halda is a family and village festival, not a public event. Visitors who come with a local host are usually welcome to watch respectfully.

faqs.q: How do I reach Keylong in January?
faqs.a: Through the Atal Tunnel from Manali, about 71 km, when the tunnel and approach roads are open to tourist vehicles. Snow often closes them, so keep spare days.

faqs.q: How cold is Keylong during Halda?
faqs.a: Very cold: night temperatures often fall well below −10 °C. Bring down clothing rated for deep winter, thermal layers, gloves and a cap.
